ketzot_hachoshen.he: ואם הגג שפל. כת' הריב"ש בסי' ת"ח וז"ל ומה שנסתפק לכם מאי איכא בין האי דאביי בשני בתי בשני צדי רה"ר דמצי אמר בני רה"ר ביממא חזי וכו' ובין אותה ששנינו בפ' חזקת אבל פותח הוא פתח כנגד פתח וחלון כנגד חלון ברה"ר דמצי אמר ליה סוף סוף בעי אצטנועי מבני רה"ר מבואר הוא דבהאי דאביי יש זמן שזה יכול לראותו בעומדו בגגו כדרכו ובני רשות הרבים אין דרך לראותו כגון בלילה אבל בהאי דפתח נגד פתח אין דרך לעמוד בתמידות בפתח ביתו ואם יעשה זה במקרה פעם אחת גם בני רשות הרבים עושין כן לפעמים כשיזדמן לדבר זה עם זה ע"ש. ולפי מה שכת' הרמ"א דאם הגג שפל עד שבני רשות הרבים רואין אותו אין כאן היזק ראיה והוא בטור בשם ר' יונה אם כן בלאו הכי לא קשה דגבי האי דפתח נגד פתח הוי ליה כמו הכא בגג שפל. וכן כת' הרב המגיד פ"ג משכנים דמיירי שהגגין גבוהין ד' אמות דאי לא שפיר קאמר ליה הא בעית אצטנועי מבני רשות הרבים וכדתנן פרק חזקת פותח פתח וכו' עכ"ל הרשב"א ז"ל ע"ש ואע"ג דבגמרא שם אמרו בני רה"ר ביממא חזי לי בלילה לא חזי לי וא"כ היכא דהגג שפל עד שבני רה"ר רואין אותן יאמר ביממא חזי לי כו' כבר כת' שם בלחם משנה דהיינו נמי דוקא היכא שגבוהין ד"א לא מצי בני רה"ר למיחזי אלא ביום שהאור רב אבל אם נמוך מד' אמות מצי בני רה"ר למיחזי בלילה כמו ביממא ע"ש:
ketzot_hachoshen.en:
Rivash distinguishes between two roofs on opposite sides of a public domain and an opening opposite an opening across a public domain. In the roof case, one owner can sometimes see the other at times when passersby ordinarily cannot, such as at night. In the doorway case, however, a person does not stand constantly in his doorway. The occasional times he does so are no different from occasions when passersby also happen to see inside.

According to Rama's ruling, if the roof is low enough that people in the public domain can ordinarily see it, there is no additional visual harm. Maggid Mishneh likewise explains that the Gemara's roof case concerns roofs at least four amot high. If they are lower, the owner can say, "You already must protect your privacy from the public." Although the Gemara mentions that people see by day but not by night, Lechem Mishneh explains that on a roof lower than four amot the public can see sufficiently even at night, whereas a higher roof may be exposed only in daylight.

מ"ש זה בצד זה ר"ל שאח' אינו גבוה מהשני (שאז עכ"פ צריכין למעקה ד"א כיון דעשוין לדירה לאפוקי אם גג א' גבוה מחבירו דאז א"צ מעקה עכ"פ גבוה ד"א כשהגג דלמטה אינו רחב לעמוד ולהציץ מרחוק וכמ"ש בטור ע"ש) דאל"כ לא הל"ל זה בצד זה כיון דמסיק דדין זה הוא ג"כ אפי' כשהן בשני צידי ר"ה אלא הל"ל הן שהן זה בצד זה הן שהן בשני צידי ר"ה גם מ"ש המחבר בסעיף שאחר זה גג הסמוך לחצר כו' נראה דפי' כן שהוא סמוך ואינו גבוה מהחצר מ"ה בעינן שיעשה עכ"פ מעקה גבוה ד"א וכמ"ש:
ומ"ש עשויים לדירה פי' שהוא מקורה ושוה ולאפוקי כשהוא משופע:
ומ"ש אפי' היו בשני צידי ר"ה. ר"ל אע"ג דבלא"ה בעי לאצטנועי מבני ר"ה העוברים ביניהן וכל' הגמ' הנ"ל וכדמסיק ג"כ המחבר וכ"ש כשהן סמוכין ועומדין זה בצד זה או זה נגד זה ורה"י עובר ביניהן וק"ל:
ומ"ש זה שלא כנגד זה ומעדיף פי' הא' עושה על גגו לרוח מזרח והב' לצד מערב וכל א' מוסיף קצת כנגד סתימת חבירו כדי שלא יראו זה את זה ע"ש בטור ונרא' דגם להרמב"ם א"צ האי העדפה אלא כשהגגין זה כנגד זה דאז יכולין להציץ זה על גג זה מן הצד אבל כשהבתים והגגין שעליהן הן זה בצד זה ממש אז אין צריך להעדפ' זו שהרי כשזה עשה החצי לצד מזרח וזה לצד מערב תכופין זה לזה שוב אין יכולין לראותו מזה לזה וק"ל:
רואה אותי תמיד פי' אפי' בלילה ואפי' כשאני יושב ואפי' בלא כוונת ראיה אלא דרך הלוכם משא"כ בני ר"ה ועד"ר ובפרישה:
meirat_einayim.en:
Two houses beside one another, etc. To explain this seif, the next, Rama's gloss there, and the beginning of siman 160, I will set out the Gemara. Bava Batra 6b states: Abaye said, two houses on opposite sides of the public domain, each builds a parapet for half his roof, not directly opposite the other's, and extends it slightly. The Gemara asks why specify the public domain, since the same should apply in a private domain, and answers that the public domain is the novelty: one might have thought that in any event each must conceal himself from passersby, so no additional wall is required. The Gemara later states in Rav Nachman's name that a roof adjacent to another roof does not require a four-amah parapet, but does require a ten-tefach partition. No one understands Abaye as disagreeing with Rav Nachman. Rambam distinguishes that Abaye deals with roofs used for dwelling, which require a four-amah parapet because of visual harm, whereas Rav Nachman deals with roofs not used for dwelling, where ten tefachim suffice so that an intruder will be caught as a thief. This is the Mechaber's meaning in seif 2 by 'between one roof and another from other roofs,' namely roofs not all used for dwelling. Rashbam and Tosafos instead distinguish by proximity. Abaye deals with roofs separated from one another, as in his example on opposite sides of a public domain. Because they are not adjacent, each person may use his roof without noticing when the other arrives, creating visual harm; therefore four amot are required. Rav Nachman deals with adjacent roofs, where each sees when the other comes and can guard his privacy, so ten tefachim suffice. The Tur follows this. This is Rama's gloss in seif 2 that some say ten tefachim suffice specifically when the roofs are adjacent, but if air separates them a parapet is required as explained above, meaning four amot as in seif 1. According to this view, even roofs used for dwelling need only ten tefachim when adjacent. With this framework the details are clear.
Beside one another. Meaning, neither is higher than the other. Otherwise, the lower roof may not require a four-amah wall if it is not wide enough for a person to stand at a distance and look over, as the Tur explains. If the Mechaber meant merely proximity, he would not have needed this phrase because he later applies the law even to roofs on opposite sides of the public domain.
Used for dwelling. Meaning, covered and level, excluding a sloped roof.
Even if they are on opposite sides of the public domain. Although each must already conceal himself from passersby below, as the Gemara says. All the more so when they are near one another or face one another across a private way.
Not directly opposite, and he extends it. One builds on the eastern half of his roof and the other on the western half, and each extends his wall slightly past the other's endpoint so they cannot see around the edges. It appears that even according to Rambam this extra extension is needed only when the roofs face one another, because then each can look sideways onto the other roof. If the houses and roofs are directly side by side, once one builds the eastern half and the other the western half right up to one another, no additional overlap is necessary.
He sees me constantly. Meaning, even at night, even while I am sitting, and even without intending to look, merely in the course of walking. Passersby in the public domain do not see in this constant manner. See the Derishah and Perishah.

turei_zahav.en: (Seif 1: when I stand.) This is difficult in light of siman 154, seif 3, where one may open a doorway to the public domain because he can say, "I am merely like one of the people in the public domain." Why can the neighbor not answer, "The public does not see me at night," as the Gemara and Tur say here? There is also a third reason in the Gemara: the public does not see me except when they deliberately look, as the Beit Yosef explains. That too should apply in siman 154. A similar difficulty exists regarding the Tur's ruling in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah, cited by the Rama, that if the roof is low, etc. One must say that the Sages were concerned mainly with the reason that the public does not see him while he is seated. The first reason, that this person sees him at night, is not a major injury because people do not ordinarily conduct their private affairs at night. Likewise, the third reason, that the public sees him only when it deliberately looks, is not a major concern, because just as the public will not commit a wrongdoing openly merely to look, so too this individual can be expected to distance himself from looking as much as possible. The Gemara lists three reasons by way of additional support. Thus the Tur writes, "when I stand during the day," mentioning the day as an added factor. The principal point, however, is whether he is standing. The Gemara's third reason is likewise only supplementary.

Abaye's rule that two roofs on opposite sides of the public domain require a parapet is because each owner does not sense the other's arrival and is therefore exposed to visual intrusion. Rav Nachman's statement that between one roof and another no parapet is required refers to adjacent roofs, where each can guard himself from private use when he sees the other owner on the roof. There is no distinction based upon whether the roof is ordinarily used for dwelling.
